claims.claim: Le Guin warns that narrative written by a poet is sometimes both over-elliptic and over-written, too aware of itself.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, answer to 'Deepthi', 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1 part 3', Book View Cafe, 2015

claims.claim: Quoting her own Steering the Craft, Le Guin says that where the passive voice belongs we ought to use it freely, calling it one of the lovely versatilities of the verb.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, answer to 'Christy', quoting Steering the Craft (2015) pp. 56-57, 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1 part 3', Book View Cafe, 2015
claims.quote: It is one of the lovely versatilities of the verb.
claims.page: Session 1 part 3, answer to Christy, quoting Steering the Craft pp. 56-57

claims.claim: Le Guin says that whatever writing schools teach, stories are not shown but told.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, answer to 'Paige', 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1', Book View Cafe, 10 August 2015
claims.quote: stories are not shown, but told

claims.claim: Le Guin says showing can be quite static whereas telling always involves moving on.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, answer to 'Paige', 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1', Book View Cafe, 10 August 2015

claims.claim: Le Guin describes limited third person as currently practised as a kind of flashlight beam giving a brilliant, narrow, simplifying intensity of vision.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, answer to 'Patricia', 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1', Book View Cafe, 10 August 2015

claims.claim: Le Guin tells writers to distrust anybody who says fiction must use only limited third person.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, answer to 'Patricia', 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1', Book View Cafe, 10 August 2015

claims.claim: Le Guin tells a writer to indulge the resonances, hints, half-repetitions, echoes and foreshadows that appear as a novel takes shape, calling a novel a living architecture.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, answer to 'Wm Henry', 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1', Book View Cafe, 10 August 2015
claims.quote: A novel is a living architecture.

claims.claim: Le Guin says description without any apparent, overt action can carry a story powerfully forward, and questions the separation of action from description as a false dichotomy.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, answer to 'Robby', 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1 continued', Book View Cafe, 2015
claims.quote: description without any apparent, overt action can carry a story

claims.claim: Le Guin says she is sick of historical novels and pastiches that are tone-deaf to the morals, the manners, the ideas and above all the language of their period.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, answer to 'Nilanjana', 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1 continued', Book View Cafe, 2015
claims.quote: above all the language of the period

claims.claim: Le Guin gives as her only rule for invented names that they avoid unpronounceable names, because the reader cannot pronounce them.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, interlineated reply to 'T.A.', 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1 part 3', Book View Cafe, 2015
claims.page: Session 1 part 3, interlineated answer to T.A.

claims.claim: Asked whether invented names need lots of apostrophes, Le Guin dismisses the device with the reply 'What for?'.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, interlineated reply to 'T.A.', 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1 part 3', Book View Cafe, 2015
claims.page: Session 1 part 3, interlineated answer to T.A.

claims.claim: Le Guin says specific features or mannerisms can help fix a minor character in the reader's mind when they turn up again.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, answer to 'Tim', 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1 continued', Book View Cafe, 2015
claims.quote: can help fix a minor character in the reader’s mind

claims.claim: Le Guin's recommendation for convincing dialogue is to read or speak it aloud, out loud rather than muttered.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, answer to 'Jacob', 'Navigating the Ocean of Story - Session 1 continued', Book View Cafe, 2015

claims.claim: Le Guin gives pronunciation guidelines for her invented names because pronunciation affects the sound and rhythm of a sentence.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Ursula on Ursula', ursulakleguin.com, undated
claims.quote: this does affect the sound and rhythm of a sentence

claims.claim: In her introduction to the revised Steering the Craft, Le Guin calls the vocabulary of grammar the names of the writer's tools.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Introduction to the revised Steering the Craft (Mariner, 2015), reproduced on ursulakleguin.com
claims.quote: these are the names of the writer’s tools

verdicts.trueWording: Narrative written by a poet is sometimes both over-elliptic and over-written — too aware of itself, not interested enough in telling the story.
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200, browser UA). Quote 'over-elliptic and over-written' present word for word in the joint answer to Joseph and Deepthi; 'too aware of itself' follows verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: Where it does belong, we ought to use it freely. It is one of the lovely versatilities of the verb.
verdicts.note: Raw page. Answer to Christy explicitly quotes Steering the Craft 'On p. 56-57'; both limbs ('we ought to use it freely', 'one of the lovely versatilities of the verb') appear verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: No matter what sacred laws the Moseses of the Iowa School of Writing handed down... stories are not shown, but told.
verdicts.note: Raw page. Answer to Paige. Quote verbatim; the 'whatever writing schools teach' limb is carried by the Iowa School of Writing clause immediately preceding it.

verdicts.trueWording: Showing can be quite static, after all; but telling always involves moving on.
verdicts.note: Raw page. Answer to Paige, final line. Both limbs verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: As currently practiced, limited third person is (like the present tense) a kind of flashlight beam — it gives a brilliant, narrow, simplifying intensity of vision.
verdicts.note: Raw page. Answer to Patricia. 'a kind of flashlight beam' verbatim; 'as currently practised' and 'brilliant, narrow, simplifying intensity of vision' both on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: Distrust anybody who says fiction must use only limited third person.
verdicts.note: Claim carries no quote field, so no verbatim test applies; the page's own sentence is near-identical: 'Distrust anybody — fellow writer, agent, editor — who tells you that fiction must use only limited third person.' Raw page, answer to Patricia.

verdicts.trueWording: ...those resonances, hints, half-repetitions, echoes, foreshadows, reminders... A novel is a living architecture.
verdicts.note: Raw page. Answer to Wm Henry opens 'Indulge, indulge! Do it!' and closes with the quoted sentence verbatim; the listed resonances appear in the same order the claim gives.

verdicts.trueWording: And description without any apparent, overt action can carry a story powerfully, irresistibly forward. ... Is this perhaps another False Dichotomy?
verdicts.note: Raw page. Answer to Robby. Quote verbatim; the false-dichotomy limb is supported by 'how do you separate action from description? Is this perhaps another False Dichotomy?'. Claim compresses 'powerfully, irresistibly forward' to 'powerfully forward' — a drop, not a distortion.

verdicts.trueWording: I'm sick of historicals and pastiches set in the historical past that are utterly, arrogantly tone-deaf to the morals, the manners, the ideas, the opportunities, and above all the language of the period.
verdicts.note: Raw page. Answer to Nilanjana, in parentheses. Quote verbatim; every listed limb present (claim omits 'the opportunities', an omission only).

verdicts.trueWording: My only 'rule': avoid unpronounceable names (like Qfwfq), because your reader can't pronounce them... and avoid sweet swoony names ending in -a (like Weena) for your heroine.
verdicts.note: Raw page, interlineated reply to T.A. 'avoid unpronounceable names' and the because-clause are verbatim, but her stated only 'rule' is a two-part one and the claim reports only the first half.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that her only rule is the pronounceability rule — the page's single 'rule' has a second, equally stated half: avoid sweet swoony names ending in -a

verdicts.note: Raw page. In the T.A. exchange 'with Ursula interlineating in italics', T.A.'s 'Lots of apostrophes?' is answered 'What for?' — verbatim, and the dismissal reading is exactly the interlineation's function.

verdicts.trueWording: Specific features or mannerisms (even absurdly specific ones!) can help fix a minor character in the reader's mind when they turn up again.
verdicts.note: Raw page. Answer to Tim. Quote verbatim including 'when they turn up again'; both the 'specific features or mannerisms' and 'minor character' limbs are the page's own words.

verdicts.trueWording: All I can recommend is to read/speak your dialogue aloud. Not whispering, not muttering, OUT LOUD.
verdicts.note: Raw page. Answer to Jacob, introduced as the answer to 'Convincing Dialogue'. Quote verbatim; the 'out loud rather than muttered' limb is the page's 'Not whispering, not muttering, OUT LOUD.'

verdicts.trueWording: And since this does affect the sound and rhythm of a sentence – and since names are magic in Earthsea – here are some guidelines.
verdicts.note: Raw page, 'How do you pronounce the names and words in your books?' section, followed by 'In my invented names and words, usually:' and the letter-by-letter guidelines. Quote verbatim. The page gives a second co-reason ('names are magic in Earthsea'); the claim asserts only the sound-and-rhythm one, which is stated, so no limb is unsupported.

verdicts.trueWording: Yet these are the names of the writer's tools.
verdicts.note: Raw page, section headed 'From the Introduction' and opening 'This is a complete revision of the book' (Mariner 2015 revision). Quote verbatim, immediately after 'the technical language of speech and writing, the vocabulary of grammar'.
